name: Virginia
summary_text: Virginia stands under the United States federal framework, and the exposures a trans visitor is most likely to meet are set at national level: identity documents, airport screening, visa decisions, federal custody and access to care. State-level conditions in Virginia are addressed separately below.  Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas, and directed the attorney general to "correct the misapplication" of Bostock v. Clayton County (2020).  The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth. New passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, while passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. In November 2025 the Supreme Court allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992.  Travellers report passports confiscated or blocked at application, with some left stranded abroad. The ACLU has sued the State Department on behalf of seven plaintiffs, and Lambda Legal maintains guidance on what documentation to consider and how name and gender changes interact with federal records.  Screening at US checkpoints carries an outing risk: TSA procedures can involve secondary screening, devices and pat-downs invasive of privacy. Several governments have responded. In April 2025 CNN reported advisories issued by several countries about trans people travelling to the United States over identity-document and data rules, and Axios reported in March 2025 that at least eight European countries, including Finland and Denmark, adjusted travel guidelines for trans and nonbinary citizens entering the country.  Facility restrictions vary sharply by state. A Movement Advancement Project tally counts state bathroom bans applying to trans people in K-12 schools and some government buildings in nine states and one territory, with outright state bans on facility use per gender identity in additional states; 29 states, four territories and the District of Columbia have no such ban, and some states make trans bathroom use a criminal offence in certain circumstances. In April 2025 a transgender student was arrested and handcuffed in a women's restroom at the Florida state capitol, which civil-rights attorneys described as the first known arrest under that state's bathroom-restriction law.  State document rules are tightening. In February 2026 Kansas enacted a law preventing transgender people from changing markers on birth certificates and driver's licences, invalidating existing documents that do not match sex assigned at birth, and barring trans people from sex-segregated facilities; rights groups call it a template for other states, with further targeting bills pending. A July 2026 national risk assessment flagged Idaho as the latest "Do Not Travel" state for trans people, bringing the total to four, and reported that the 2026 legislative season continued to degrade trans rights while federal policies drove nationwide trends.  Visa screening carries its own exposure. Executive Order 14201 of 5 February 2025 was followed on 25 February 2025 by a State Department announcement refusing visas to trans athletes entering the United States to compete in women's sporting events; applicants are flagged with the internal marking "SWS25", and listing a gender other than one's assigned sex is treated as grounds for a permanent ban on fraud grounds.  Federal custody presents documented harm. From 2026 the Federal Bureau of Prisons adopted Florida-based policies mandating conversion therapy for transgender inmates, including cutting hair short, withdrawing hormone medication and substituting psychiatric therapy and drugs; imprisoned transgender people reported denial of care, and the Bureau stopped reporting the number of transgender prisoners held from 2025. In ICE custody, transgender men were reportedly subjected to forced-labour programmes with refusals met by beatings, solitary confinement and reports of severe sexual abuse. In December 2025 the Attorney General instructed the FBI to offer cash bounties for information leading to the identification and arrest of transgender activists described as promoting "radical gender ideology" and characterised as "domestic terrorist groups"; a May 2026 White House counterterrorism strategy stated that activities would prioritise the identification and neutralisation of groups whose ideology is "anti-American, radically pro-transgender, and anarchist." Advocates have compared these actions to the early stages of genocide.  Care access is constrained. Executive Order 14187 of January 2025 described gender-affirming care for minors as "chemical and surgical mutilation of children," leading some hospitals to pause care; in summer 2025 the Department of Justice subpoenaed over 20 hospitals for full records of patients under 19. In July 2025 the federal government shut down specialised LGBTQ youth services on the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, and October 2025 proposed rules would bar Medicaid reimbursement for care to transgender patients under 18. Gender-affirming care for children is banned in 27 states. Several of these federal measures have been blocked or enjoined in court.  Virginia itself sits in the Low-Risk States group of the July 2026 national legal risk assessment, alongside Arizona, Delaware, Maine, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and the District of Columbia. The same assessment names Virginia with Arizona as a state that enacted youth-targeting anti-trans policies which, because of state-specific factors, appear unlikely to extend to adults.

name: West Virginia
summary_text: Every visitor to West Virginia stands first under the federal travel-document regime. Executive Order 14168, signed 20 January 2025, redefined sex for federal purposes as a male-female binary, barred transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with their gender identity, and prohibited self-selection of gender on passports and visas. The State Department stopped processing the X marker and any marker not matching sex assigned at birth; new passport applications are processed only as M or F according to supporting documents, and passports already issued with an X marker remain valid until they expire. The Supreme Court in November 2025 allowed the passport sex-marker restrictions to take effect, superseding a State Department policy in place since 1992. A trans or nonbinary visitor can therefore arrive holding papers that do not match their presentation, with airport screening and visa decisions following the same national rules, including the February 2025 State Department policy refusing visas to trans athletes seeking entry to compete in women's sporting events and treating applicants who list a gender other than their assigned sex as grounds for a permanent ban for fraud.  West Virginia's own facility restriction is statutory. Governor Patrick Morrisey signed Senate Bill 456, the 'Riley Gaines Act,' on 12 March 2025, after the state Senate passed it on 3 March and the House of Delegates passed it on 6 March. The statute defines 'woman' as an adult human of the female sex and 'man' as an adult human of the male sex and aims to preserve women's single-sex spaces, covering locker rooms, bathrooms, rape crisis centers, dormitories, prisons, and domestic violence shelters. At the signing, Morrisey said bathrooms, locker rooms, domestic violence shelters and rape crisis centers 'should be kept private for women only.' The Movement Advancement Project equality map cataloguing state bans on transgender people's use of public bathrooms and facilities according to their gender identity is the source for West Virginia's facility-ban enumeration.  National risk gradings place West Virginia near the top of the risk scale. The July 2026 Anti-Trans National Legal Risk Assessment Map (Erin In The Morning, published 27 August 2026) places West Virginia in 'The Worst States' group (AL, AR, IA, IN, LA, MS, OH, OK, ND, SC, SD, TN, UT, WV, WY), one tier below 'Do Not Travel' (FL, ID, KS, TX), within a national frame of 'Worst Policies In Effect'. Idaho was promoted to 'Do Not Travel' as the fourth such state after its felony bathroom ban, which carries up to 5 years and is partially court-blocked but in force wherever no gender-neutral option exists.

sources.title: Bostock v. Clayton County - U.S. Supreme Court
sources.documents: Establishes that workplace discrimination on basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is sex discrimination under Title VII, providing federal employment protection for LGBTQ people in West Virginia where state statutes do not address it.
sources.detail: Cited as decided June 15, 2020, consolidated with Altitude Express, Inc. v. Zarda and R.G. & G.R. Harris Funeral Homes Inc. v. EEOC; no URL visible in text.
